evidence_quotes.quote: These datasets have a nationally representative sample and include information on primary drinking water sources as well as household characteristics relating to sanitation and access to technologies.

The indicators relate to the dwelling itself (type, ownership), access to electricity (source of lighting), access to sanitation services (type of toilet, liquid and solid waste disposal methods, type of water used for non-drinking purposes), type of cooking fuel, and access to technology (mobile phone, computer).
Indeed, there is a need for further empirical research towards effective water governance in Africa’s rapidly expanding cities and towns [3].
Trends in development from both the census data and the SHDI were regressed against trends in changing drinking water sources over the study period using repeated measures correlation [45].

By the end of the study period in 2017, sachet water was consumed by 35% of households as their primary source of drinking water, mostly driven by increasing consumption in urban areas. The consumption of piped water decreased from 46% of households in 2010 to 27% in 2017, corresponding to a fall of around 750,000 households in absolute terms (S1 Fig).

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking water and domestic non-drinking water sources (sachet water, private and public piped water, groundwater, and unimproved sources) as well as household sanitation characteristics in Ghana from 2010 to 2017.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study does not empirically examine any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor; its empirical analysis correlates spatiotemporal trends in sachet water consumption only with household living-standard proxies and Subnational Human Development Index (SHDI) metrics, while water governance failures, cost recovery, FDA quality inspection seals, and participatory governance are discussed purely as unanalysed background and policy commentary in the Introduction and Discussion. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, no rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules, tariff rules, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure) is empirically analysed; although dwelling ownership (owned vs. renting/rent-free/perching) is included among 11 household living-standard indicators, it is treated solely as a socioeconomic wealth/living-standards proxy in regional correlations rather than a tenure or documentation rule governing water connection or access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains quantitative empirical evidence using three nationally representative surveys (the 10% sample of the 2010 Population and Housing Census, the 2013 GLSS6, and the 2017 GLSS7) combined with spatial autocorrelation (global and local Moran's I / LISA) and regional repeated-measures correlation analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household-level proportions and counts of primary drinking water sources (sachet water, piped water, groundwater, surface water, and JMP improved vs. unimproved classifications) and domestic non-drinking water sources across urban/rural areas, 170 districts, and 10 regions.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (households in Ghana aggregated to 170 districts and 10 administrative regions across 2010, 2013, and 2017), empirical correlates/exposures (socioeconomic living-standard proxies and regional SHDI indicators), outcomes (primary drinking water source shares), and study design (repeated cross-sectional spatiotemporal and correlational design) are clearly reported, though the exposure is socioeconomic/demographic rather than legal or regulatory.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

study_design: Repeated cross-sectional spatiotemporal and regional correlational study
population_and_sample: Households in Ghana drawn from three nationally representative surveys: 2010 Population and Housing Census 10% public sample (37,642 enumeration areas), 2013 Ghana Living Standards Survey (GLSS6), and 2017 GLSS7, harmonised to 170 districts and 10 administrative regions (30 region-year data points for repeated-measures correlation)
exposure: Spatiotemporal location (district/region, urban/rural, 2010–2017), household living-standard proxy characteristics (dwelling type and ownership, lighting, toilet type, cooking fuel, solid and liquid waste disposal, computer and mobile phone access, non-drinking water source, gender of household head), and Subnational Human Development Index (SHDI, GNI, education index, health index)
outcome: Household primary source of drinking water (sachet water vs. piped water, groundwater, and unimproved surface water sources) and primary water source for domestic non-drinking uses
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While this repeated cross-sectional study empirically examines household drinking water sources (sachet water vs. piped and other sources) across Ghana from 2010 to 2017, its empirical explanatory variables are strictly demographic, geographic, and socioeconomic living-standard proxies alongside regional human development indices. Water governance, regulation of packaged water, and cost recovery are discussed only as unanalysed background and policy commentary in the Introduction and Discussion, so the study fails Criterion 2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading.
